title: LangGraph: Checkpoints, Streaming & Human-in-the-Loop
summary: A stateful graph becomes durable when you attach a checkpointer: it snapshots state after each step under a thread_id, so runs survive crashes and can be resumed or time-traveled. The same persistence enables streaming intermediate events and human-in-the-loop interrupts that pause the graph for approval and resume where they left off. The classic bug: no checkpointer or a mismatched thread_id, so state silently resets.

subtopics.title: Checkpointers persist state after every step
subtopics.explanation: A checkpointer is a storage backend (in-memory for dev, SQLite/Postgres for production) passed to compile() that saves a snapshot of the graph's state after each node runs. This turns an ephemeral run into a durable one that can survive process restarts. Attaching a checkpointer is the single switch that unlocks resuming, streaming state, and human-in-the-loop, so it is the foundation of every feature in this topic.
subtopics.example:
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

# dev: in-memory; prod: SqliteSaver / PostgresSaver
checkpointer = MemorySaver()
app = graph.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)
# now every step's state is snapshotted and resumable

subtopics.title: thread_id groups checkpoints into a conversation
subtopics.explanation: With a checkpointer, every invoke/stream call must pass a config with a thread_id; all checkpoints sharing that id form one continuous thread, so a second call with the same id continues from the saved state. Use a new thread_id for a new independent run and the same id to continue an existing one. This id is the key that ties persisted state to a specific user or conversation, and getting it wrong is the number-one cause of 'my agent forgot everything'.
subtopics.example:
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42"}}

app.invoke({"messages": ["hi"]}, config)
# later, SAME thread_id -> continues from saved state
app.invoke({"messages": ["and again"]}, config)
# a DIFFERENT thread_id would start a fresh, empty run

subtopics.title: Resuming and time travel
subtopics.explanation: Because state is snapshotted per step, you can inspect the latest checkpoint with get_state, list the history, and even resume from an earlier checkpoint to explore an alternate path ('time travel'). Resuming after a crash means invoking again with the same thread_id; the graph picks up from the last completed node instead of restarting. This ability to replay and branch from any past step is what makes long-running or fragile agents debuggable and fault-tolerant.
subtopics.example:
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42"}}

snapshot = app.get_state(config)      # latest saved state
print(snapshot.values, snapshot.next) # data + next node(s)

# resume after a crash: same thread_id, no new input needed
app.invoke(None, config)              # continues from checkpoint

subtopics.title: Streaming intermediate events
subtopics.explanation: Instead of waiting for the final result, stream() yields updates as the graph progresses, using modes like 'values' (full state after each step) or 'updates' (just each node's changes), and token-level streaming for LLM output. This is how you build responsive UIs that show the agent thinking rather than a spinner. Streaming reads the same per-step state the checkpointer saves, so it is a natural companion to persistence rather than a separate mechanism.

subtopics.title: Interrupts pause the graph for a human
subtopics.explanation: Human-in-the-loop is built on interrupts: you configure the graph to pause before (or after) a sensitive node, or call interrupt() inside a node, which halts execution and persists state. A human reviews or edits the state, then you resume with a Command (or another invoke with the same thread_id) to continue. Interrupts only work because state is checkpointed, so approval workflows are really 'pause, persist, resume' — the safety valve for agents that take real-world actions.
subtopics.example:
from langgraph.types import Command

# compile with a pause before the risky tool node
app = graph.compile(checkpointer=cp, interrupt_before=["execute_tool"])
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42"}}

app.invoke({"action": "delete_account"}, config)  # pauses here
# human approves, then resume from the checkpoint:
app.invoke(Command(resume="approved"), config)

foundations.overview: In LangGraph, persistence is the feature that turns a stateful graph into a durable, interactive system. You attach a checkpointer at compile time — MemorySaver for development, SqliteSaver or PostgresSaver for production — and the graph automatically snapshots its full state after every node executes. Those snapshots are grouped by a thread_id passed in the run config, so all checkpoints under one id form a single continuous thread (a conversation or a run). This unlocks three capabilities that share the same substrate. Resuming and time travel: you can read the current state with get_state, replay history, resume from the last checkpoint after a crash by invoking with the same thread_id, or branch from an earlier step. Streaming: stream() yields intermediate events — full state ('values'), per-node deltas ('updates'), or LLM tokens — reading the very state the checkpointer records, so UIs can show progress live. Human-in-the-loop: interrupts (via interrupt_before/after or an in-node interrupt() call) pause the graph and persist state so a person can approve or edit before you resume with a Command. The unifying idea: persistence is not one feature but the layer everything else stands on. The dominant failure is forgetting the checkpointer or passing an inconsistent thread_id, which makes state silently reset.
foundations.formalDefinition: A checkpointer is a persistence backend that stores an immutable snapshot of graph state (channel values plus pending next-node metadata) after each superstep, keyed by (thread_id, checkpoint_id). A thread is the ordered sequence of checkpoints under one thread_id. Resuming re-enters the graph from the latest (or a chosen) checkpoint; streaming emits per-step state as it is produced; an interrupt is a checkpoint that halts execution pending external input, resumed with a Command carrying that input.
foundations.whyItMatters: Real agents run long, call fallible tools, and sometimes must ask a human before acting. Without persistence, a crash loses everything, there is no way to show progress, and no safe pause point for approval. Checkpointing makes agents fault-tolerant, observable, and controllable — the difference between a demo and something you can run against production systems.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the checkpointer as a save-game system and thread_id as the save slot. After every move the game auto-saves to your slot; loading the same slot continues your game, while a different slot starts a new one. Streaming is watching the moves happen live rather than only seeing the end screen, and an interrupt is the game pausing to ask 'are you sure?' before a destructive action, waiting on the same save until you answer.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Chat agents persist per-user conversations by thread_id; long research or coding agents resume after crashes instead of restarting; UIs stream 'updates' to show the agent's steps in real time; and approval workflows interrupt before irreversible tool calls (refunds, deletions, deploys) so a human signs off before execution continues.
foundations.performanceImpact: Checkpointing adds a write per superstep, so latency depends on the backend (in-memory is trivial; Postgres adds a round trip) and on state size — keep state lean and avoid stuffing large blobs into channels. Streaming has negligible overhead and improves perceived latency by showing progress; the checkpoint write is the main cost, mitigated by fast storage and small state.
commonUseCases: Per-user conversational memory keyed by thread_id
Crash-resilient long-running agents that resume mid-run
Live-progress UIs via streamed node updates or tokens
Approval gates that interrupt before irreversible actions

commonMisconceptions.myth: State persists automatically once the graph is stateful.
commonMisconceptions.reality: State only persists if you attach a checkpointer at compile time. Without one, each invoke starts from the input you pass and nothing is saved between calls.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Any thread_id works as long as you pass one.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Continuity depends on reusing the SAME thread_id. A new or randomly generated id per call creates a fresh empty thread, so the agent appears to forget everything.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Interrupts are a separate feature from checkpointing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Interrupts require a checkpointer — pausing works by saving state and halting, then resuming from that checkpoint. No checkpointer means no working human-in-the-loop.

interactiveExamples.title: Same thread_id remembers; a new one forgets
interactiveExamples.explanation: A tiny counting graph with a MemorySaver checkpointer and an append reducer. Invoking twice with the same thread_id accumulates, but a fresh thread_id starts empty — the core intuition behind persistence.

code.code:
from typing import TypedDict, Annotated
from operator import add
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

class State(TypedDict):
    events: Annotated[list[str], add]

def step(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"events": [f"event {len(state['events']) + 1}"]}

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("step", step)
g.add_edge(START, "step")
g.add_edge("step", END)
app = g.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())   # persistence on

same = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "A"}}
app.invoke({"events": []}, same)
print(app.invoke({"events": []}, same)["events"])   # continues thread A

fresh = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "B"}}
print(app.invoke({"events": []}, fresh)["events"])  # new empty thread
code.caption: Thread A accumulates across two calls; thread B is independent and starts fresh — the thread_id is the memory key.

interactiveExamples.title: Interrupt before a risky node, then resume
interactiveExamples.explanation: Compile with interrupt_before on a sensitive node so the graph pauses; get_state shows it is waiting, and resuming with the same thread_id (no new input) runs the paused node. This is the shape of every approval workflow.

code.code:
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

class State(TypedDict):
    action: str
    status: str

def prepare(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"status": "pending approval"}

def execute(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"status": f"executed: {state['action']}"}

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("prepare", prepare)
g.add_node("execute", execute)
g.add_edge(START, "prepare")
g.add_edge("prepare", "execute")
g.add_edge("execute", END)
# pause right before the sensitive 'execute' node
app = g.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver(), interrupt_before=["execute"])

cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "t1"}}
app.invoke({"action": "deploy", "status": ""}, cfg)   # pauses before execute
print(app.get_state(cfg).values["status"])            # 'pending approval'
print(app.get_state(cfg).next)                        # ('execute',)

# human approved -> resume with same thread_id, no new input
final = app.invoke(None, cfg)
print(final["status"])
code.caption: The graph halts before 'execute' and persists; get_state reveals the pending next node; invoking with None resumes from the checkpoint.

debuggingLab.title: The agent forgets everything between turns
debuggingLab.symptom: A multi-turn chat agent never remembers prior messages: each turn responds as if the conversation just started, even though the state uses an append reducer for messages. In a second variant, a checkpointer IS attached but a fresh thread_id is generated on every call, with the same forgetful result.

brokenCode.code:
import uuid
from typing import TypedDict, Annotated
from operator import add
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END

class State(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list[str], add]

def reply(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"messages": [f"saw {len(state['messages'])} prior msg(s)"]}

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("reply", reply)
g.add_edge(START, "reply")
g.add_edge("reply", END)

# BUG 1: no checkpointer -> nothing is ever persisted
app = g.compile()

def turn(user_msg: str):
    # BUG 2: a NEW thread_id every call -> even with a checkpointer,
    #        each turn is an isolated, empty thread
    cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": str(uuid.uuid4())}}
    return app.invoke({"messages": [user_msg]}, cfg)["messages"]

print(turn("hello"))
print(turn("still there?"))   # expected to remember, but doesn't

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Two independent defects cause the same 'amnesia'. First, g.compile() has no checkpointer, so LangGraph keeps no state between separate invoke calls — every turn begins from only the input dict you pass, and the append reducer only accumulates within a single run, not across runs. Second, even after adding a checkpointer, the code mints a brand-new thread_id (uuid4) on every turn; since continuity is keyed by thread_id, each call reads and writes a different, empty thread. Persistence needs BOTH a checkpointer AND a stable thread_id per conversation; missing either one makes the agent stateless.
commonMistakes: Believing an append reducer gives cross-call memory — reducers only merge within one run; durability comes from the checkpointer.
Generating a random thread_id per request instead of tying it to the user/conversation, silently starting a fresh thread each time.
Attaching the checkpointer but forgetting to pass any config/thread_id at invoke time, which errors or defaults to no continuity.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Attach a MemorySaver (or a production SqliteSaver/PostgresSaver) at compile time AND derive the thread_id from a stable conversation key so successive turns share the same thread and accumulate history.

solution.code:
from typing import TypedDict, Annotated
from operator import add
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

class State(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list[str], add]

def reply(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"messages": [f"saw {len(state['messages'])} prior msg(s)"]}

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("reply", reply)
g.add_edge(START, "reply")
g.add_edge("reply", END)

# FIX 1: attach a checkpointer so state survives between invokes
app = g.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())

def turn(user_msg: str, conversation_id: str):
    # FIX 2: stable thread_id tied to the conversation, not random
    cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": conversation_id}}
    return app.invoke({"messages": [user_msg]}, cfg)["messages"]

print(turn("hello", "conv-1"))
print(turn("still there?", "conv-1"))   # same thread -> remembers

debuggingLab.expectedOutput:
['hello', 'saw 1 prior msg(s)']
['hello', 'saw 1 prior msg(s)', 'still there?', 'saw 3 prior msg(s)']

checkpoints.prompt: What is required for a LangGraph app's state to persist across separate invoke() calls?
options: An append reducer on every field
A checkpointer attached at compile time plus a consistent thread_id
checkpoints.explanation: Durability comes from compiling with a checkpointer AND reusing the same thread_id. Reducers only merge within a single run; streaming and get_state read state but don't create persistence.

checkpoints.prompt: You attach a checkpointer but generate a new random thread_id on every request. What happens?
options: The graph errors on the second call
Each call reads/writes a fresh empty thread, so the agent appears to forget everything
checkpoints.explanation: Continuity is keyed by thread_id. A new id per call points at a new empty thread, so despite the checkpointer, nothing carries over — a very common 'my agent has amnesia' bug.

checkpoints.prompt: With a MemorySaver and an append-reducer 'x', these two invokes share thread_id 't'. What prints?
checkpoints.code:
# x: Annotated[list, operator.add]; node appends one item per run
cfg = {'configurable': {'thread_id': 't'}}
app.invoke({'x': []}, cfg)
print(len(app.invoke({'x': []}, cfg)['x']))
checkpoints.explanation: The first invoke saves one item to thread 't'; the second invoke (same id) resumes from that saved state and appends another, so the length is 2.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the compile call so the graph pauses before the 'charge_card' node for human approval.
checkpoints.explanation: interrupt_before=[...] tells LangGraph to halt and persist state just before the named node(s), so a human can review before you resume with the same thread_id. It only works because a checkpointer is attached.

theory.question: How does persistence work in LangGraph, and what roles do the checkpointer and thread_id play?
theory.directAnswer: You attach a checkpointer at compile time (MemorySaver for dev, SqliteSaver/PostgresSaver for prod) and it snapshots the full graph state after each node runs. Every checkpoint is keyed by the thread_id passed in the run config, so all checkpoints under one id form a single continuous thread. Reusing that thread_id resumes from the saved state; a different id starts a fresh run. Both pieces are required — the checkpointer to store snapshots, the thread_id to identify which thread to read and write.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A per-step snapshotting layer: state (channel values plus pending next nodes) is saved after each superstep to a backend, grouped by thread_id.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Long-running, fallible, interactive agents need to survive crashes, show progress, and pause for approval — none of which is possible if state is discarded when a call returns.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: compile(checkpointer=...) enables writes; each invoke/stream passes {'configurable': {'thread_id': id}}; the graph loads the latest checkpoint for that thread, runs, and writes new checkpoints. get_state reads the latest, and resuming re-enters from it.

theory.whyImportant: Persistence is the foundation for resuming, streaming, and human-in-the-loop — all three read or halt on the same checkpointed state, so understanding it explains the entire feature set.
theory.realWorldExample: A support chatbot uses the customer's conversation id as thread_id; every turn resumes the same thread so the agent remembers earlier messages, and a crash mid-turn resumes from the last checkpoint instead of losing the conversation.

followUps.question: Why isn't an append reducer enough for cross-call memory?
followUps.answer: Reducers only merge writes within a single run; between separate invokes, only the checkpointer persists state, and only when the same thread_id is reused.

followUps.question: What backend would you use in production and why?
followUps.answer: A durable store like PostgresSaver (or SqliteSaver for smaller scale) so checkpoints survive restarts and can be shared across processes, unlike the in-memory MemorySaver used for development.

theory.question: Explain how human-in-the-loop interrupts work in LangGraph and why they depend on checkpointing.
theory.directAnswer: You either compile with interrupt_before/interrupt_after naming sensitive nodes, or call interrupt() inside a node. Execution halts at that point and the current state is persisted as a checkpoint; the invoke call returns without finishing. A human inspects or edits the state, then you resume by invoking again with the same thread_id (passing a Command with the human's input, or None to just continue). It depends on checkpointing because 'pausing' is literally saving state and stopping — without a checkpointer there is nothing to save or resume from.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A controlled pause-and-resume mechanism that yields control to a human at defined points, backed by the persistence layer.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Agents increasingly take irreversible real-world actions (payments, deletions, deploys); a safe system must let a human approve or correct before those actions execute.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The interrupt creates a checkpoint marking the next node as pending and returns. get_state shows the pending node. Resuming re-enters from that checkpoint; a Command(resume=...) injects the human's decision, and the graph continues (or takes an alternate branch) from exactly where it paused.

theory.whyImportant: It is the primary safety valve for autonomous agents, turning 'the agent might do something bad' into 'the agent asks first', and it showcases why persistence underpins everything.
theory.realWorldExample: A finance agent prepares a refund, interrupts before the 'issue_refund' node, and waits; an operator approves in a UI, the app resumes with Command(resume='approved'), and only then is the refund executed.

followUps.question: Can the human edit state, not just approve?
followUps.answer: Yes — you can update the checkpointed state (e.g. correct a tool argument) before resuming, so the graph continues with the human-corrected values.

followUps.question: What happens to an interrupt if there's no checkpointer?
followUps.answer: It can't work — there's no place to save the paused state, so the pause/resume cycle has nothing to resume from.

scenario.question: Users report that your LangGraph chat agent 'forgets' the conversation between messages, and a long-running research agent restarts from scratch after any crash. How do you diagnose and fix both?
scenario.directAnswer: Both are persistence failures. First confirm a checkpointer is attached at compile time; if not, add a durable one (Postgres/SQLite in prod). Then verify the thread_id is stable per conversation/run rather than regenerated each call — the classic bug is minting a new uuid every request. With a checkpointer plus a stable thread_id, chat turns accumulate and the research agent resumes from its last checkpoint by invoking with the same thread_id after a crash.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A diagnosis of lost state traced to the two persistence prerequisites: the checkpointer and a consistent thread_id.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It's easy to enable one without the other — a stateful graph and append reducers create the illusion of memory that only holds within a single run, so the gap surfaces only across calls or after a crash.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Inspect compile() for a checkpointer; log the thread_id used per request to confirm it's derived from a stable key (user/conversation id), not random; use get_state to verify checkpoints exist for that thread; for crash recovery, on restart invoke(None, config) with the same thread_id to resume from the last saved step.

scenario.whyImportant: These are the two most common LangGraph production bugs, and both are silent — the app runs fine but behaves statelessly, so knowing to check checkpointer-plus-thread_id saves hours of misdirected debugging.
scenario.realWorldExample: A team's agent used MemorySaver and generated a fresh thread_id per HTTP request; switching to PostgresSaver and keying thread_id on the session id fixed both the amnesia and enabled crash resume.

followUps.question: Why not just keep history in a global variable?
followUps.answer: It breaks under concurrency and multiple processes, isn't tied to a specific conversation, and loses everything on restart — the checkpointer solves all three.

followUps.question: How would you resume specifically after a mid-run crash?
followUps.answer: Invoke with the same thread_id and no new input (invoke(None, config)); the graph re-enters from the last checkpoint and finishes the remaining nodes.

coding.question: Write a LangGraph app with a checkpointer and an append-reducer 'turns' field, plus a chat(app, msg, conv_id) helper that invokes with a stable thread_id so successive calls for the same conv_id accumulate turns.
coding.thoughtProcess: Memory across calls needs a checkpointer, so I compile with MemorySaver. The 'turns' field uses operator.add to accumulate within and across runs. The chat helper must build the config from conv_id (not a random id) and reuse it, so calls with the same conv_id continue the same thread while different conv_ids stay isolated.
lineByLine: 'turns' is Annotated with operator.add so entries accumulate rather than overwrite.
build() compiles WITH MemorySaver, which is what persists state between separate chat() calls.
chat() derives the config's thread_id from conv_id, so it's stable across calls for the same conversation.
Invoking with the same conv_id resumes the saved thread and appends, while a new conv_id starts an isolated empty thread.
The __main__ block shows c1 growing across two calls and c2 starting fresh, proving isolation by thread_id.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) graph work per call plus the checkpointer's read/write cost (constant for MemorySaver, a round trip for a DB backend).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(t) per thread, where t is the number of accumulated turns stored in that thread's checkpoints.

followUps.question: How would you make this survive a process restart?
followUps.answer: Swap MemorySaver for a durable backend like SqliteSaver or PostgresSaver so checkpoints persist to disk/DB and can be reloaded by a new process.

followUps.question: How would you add an approval step before responding?
followUps.answer: Compile with interrupt_before=['respond'] so the graph pauses and persists; a human approves, then you resume with the same conv_id via invoke(None, cfg) or a Command.

keyTakeaways: Attach a checkpointer at compile time to snapshot state after every step — MemorySaver for dev, SqliteSaver/PostgresSaver for production.
Continuity is keyed by thread_id: reuse the same id to resume/accumulate, use a new id for an independent run; a random id per call causes silent amnesia.
Persistence enables resuming after crashes and time travel (get_state, replay, branch from an earlier checkpoint) with the same thread_id.
Streaming (stream_mode 'values'/'updates'/tokens) surfaces intermediate state for responsive UIs, reading the same state the checkpointer records.
Human-in-the-loop interrupts (interrupt_before/after or interrupt()) pause and persist for approval, then resume with a Command — they only work because state is checkpointed.
